meta.title: Who really said "Damn it, Jim! I'm a doctor, not a.."? | Quotle.info
meta.description: McCoy never said "Damn it, Jim" — the word was taboo on 1960s TV. Gene L. Coon wrote the real line for Star Trek in 1967: "I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer!"
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Damn it, Jim! I'm a doctor, not a..'?
meta.ogDescription: The censors banned "damn," so parodists added it. The real line, by writer Gene L. Coon: "I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer!" — Star Trek, 9 March 1967.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer!”
answer.authorDates: 1924–1973 · Star Trek screenwriter, story editor & showrunner
answer.sourceLine: Dr. McCoy’s catchphrase was born in “The Devil in the Dark” (Star Trek, 9 March 1967), written by Gene L. Coon: Kirk orders McCoy to treat a silicon-based creature and McCoy snaps, “I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer!” He never says “Damn it” — the word was taboo on 1960s network television — and he doesn't say “Jim” in the line either. Both halves of the popular wording are later accretions.

source.heading: The line as broadcast

docMeta.dd: Star Trek, season 1, episode 25 — “The Devil in the Dark”
Gene L. Coon (directed by Joseph Pevney)
Dr. Leonard “Bones” McCoy (DeForest Kelley) — a fictional character

source.excerpt:
McCoy: You can't be serious. That thing is virtually made out of stone!
Kirk: Help it. Treat it.
McCoy: I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer!
Kirk: You're a healer. There's a patient. That's an order.
trail: 1966 — the seed. Gene L. Coon drafts his story outline for “The Devil in the Dark” on 29 November 1966. Per StarTrek.com ↗ the phrase appears there as plain description — “He is a doctor, not a bricklayer” — and is then “reformatted and used by the good doctor himself in the script as dialogue.” The line is authored, not borrowed and not improvised.

1967 — broadcast. The episode airs 9 March 1967. Wikipedia ↗: “This episode marks the first appearance of Doctor McCoy's catchphrase, ‘I'm a doctor, not a ...’” It recurs throughout the run; Memory Alpha ↗ catalogues the variants — psychiatrist, escalator, mechanic, engineer, coal miner. None carries an oath.

The drift. Wikiquote ↗ lists the popular wording under Misattributed, alongside “Beam me up, Scotty” and “She can't take much more of this, Captain” — a whole shelf of Star Trek lines the public quotes and the series never contained. The common thread: each is a tidier, punchier sentence than the one actually broadcast.

2016 — the misquote comes true. Memory Alpha ↗ records that “this version of the line was eventually used” by the alternate-reality McCoy: Karl Urban, in Star Trek Beyond (written by Simon Pegg and Doug Jung), reaches “Damn it, Jim, I'm a doctor, not a fu –” and is beamed out before finishing.
source.excerptNote: Kirk has just ordered McCoy to treat the Horta, a wounded silicon-based lifeform. Note what isn't there: no oath, and no “Jim.” Wikipedia records this as the first appearance of the catchphrase; every later variant — escalator, mechanic, engineer, coal miner — is built on this one.

source.rightsHolder: Paramount Global — successor to Norway Productions and Desilu Productions, which produced the series in this period; CBS Media Ventures holds the Star Trek television rights
source.rightsNote: “The Devil in the Dark” was first broadcast in 1967, well after the 1930 US public-domain cutoff, so it remains in copyright. Television writing is work-for-hire: the rights belong to the studio, not to Gene L. Coon's estate. Per Wikipedia ↗, “Norway Productions and Desilu Productions produced the series from September 1966 to December 1967” — the window this episode falls in — with the franchise television rights now held by CBS Media Ventures under Paramount Global. The short quoted exchange above is reproduced for identification and commentary.

author.name: Gene L. Coon
author.kicker: The writer of the real line
author.heading: The man who wrote Bones
author.metaLine: 1924–1973 · Star Trek screenwriter, story editor & showrunner
author.bio: Gene L. Coon (7 January 1924 – 8 July 1973) was the screenwriter, story editor and showrunner who ran Star Trek from the middle of its first season to the middle of its second — the stretch in which much of the show's enduring furniture was invented. He is credited with creating the Klingons, Khan Noonien Singh and Zefram Cochrane, with advancing the Prime Directive, and with formally naming the United Federation of Planets and Starfleet Command. He also wrote “The Devil in the Dark,” the episode that gave Leonard McCoy the complaint he would be quoted on — usually incorrectly — for the next sixty years.

misattribution.heading: What's actually wrong here
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited on this one. The show is right, the character is right, the actor is right — the words are wrong, in three separate places, and the writer gets forgotten.

items.why: Wikiquote files “Damn it, Jim! I'm a doctor not a...” under Misattributed ↗, noting McCoy “never uttered ‘Damn it’ during the series; the closest he or anyone ever came was the euphemisms ‘Blast it!’ or ‘Blast!’” Wikipedia's article on Leonard McCoy ↗ agrees: “damn” was considered taboo on 1960s television.
In the transcribed exchange ↗ McCoy is indeed snapping at Kirk, but the line itself names nobody: “I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer!” The “Jim” is supplied by memory.

Kelley spoke the line; he did not write it. StarTrek.com's account of the episode's development ↗ shows the phrase originating in Gene L. Coon's own story outline, typed as description — “He is a doctor, not a bricklayer” — before being “reformatted and used by the good doctor himself in the script as dialogue.”

A popular retelling holds that the catchphrase began as an improvisation. The version we could find cites only “accounts from the show's production” ↗ with no named witness or document. A dated story outline in the writer's hand outranks an unsourced anecdote.

CBR canvasses the likely culprits — a Saturday Night Live Star Trek sketch, and Jay Leno's 1984 routine — but offers them as speculation rather than a finding ↗. We have not seen the misquote's first appearance pinned to a specific broadcast, and we don't assert one.

misattribution.truthLine: Gene L. Coon wrote it, DeForest Kelley said it, and what he said was “I'm a doctor, not a bricklayer! ↗” — no oath, no Jim. Curiously, the popular wording did eventually reach the screen: Karl Urban's McCoy gets as far as “Damn it, Jim, I'm a doctor, not a fu –” ↗ in Star Trek Beyond (2016) before being beamed out mid-word.

context.heading: Why the words drifted
lead: McCoy’s complaint was never a fixed sentence — it was a template. Across three seasons DeForest Kelley filled the blank with bricklayer, escalator, mechanic, engineer, coal miner, psychiatrist, magician. Wikiquote's own page files it under repeated lines as “I'm a doctor, not a ______________!” A phrase with a hole in the middle is remembered as a shape rather than as words, and shapes are easy to reupholster.

What got added was the swearing. “Damn” was effectively unsayable on 1960s American network television, so the writers reached for “Blast it!” instead. But parodists were under no such constraint, and the profanity that Kelley was forbidden migrated back onto him through decades of impressions — until the quotation people confidently recite is one the censors had specifically prohibited.
context.detailsSummary: The joke came full circle in 2016
detailsBody: The Kelvin-timeline films let Karl Urban’s McCoy do what Kelley could not. Memory Alpha records “Damn it, man, I'm a doctor, not a physicist!” in Star Trek (2009) and “Damn it, man, I'm a doctor, not a torpedo technician!” in Star Trek Into Darkness (2013) — both addressed to “man,” not to Jim.

The full popular wording finally reached the screen in Star Trek Beyond (2016), written by Simon Pegg and Doug Jung. Memory Alpha transcribes it as “Damn it, Jim, I'm a doctor, not a fu –” — McCoy is beamed out mid-word. After half a century of being quoted saying it, the character got to say it exactly once, and was not allowed to finish.
context.pull: The censors banned the word. The impressionists put it back. The public kept the impressionists’ version.
